storm.summary_layperson: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms is tracking in from the northwest this evening, and unlike many summer nights here, the Sound's usual storm-weakening effect isn't strong enough to engage tonight, so expect the cove to get hit close to full strength, in line with surrounding towns.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Air-water gap is 9°F right now, just under the 10°F threshold the marine layer needs to engage, and it fades toward zero by 8 PM anyway — no local buffer for tonight's storms.
storm.detail_html:
A scattered-to-broken line of showers and thunderstorms is tracking west to east across the region between roughly 6 PM and 10 PM tonight, per the NWS Upton area forecast discussion. A Severe Thunderstorm Watch covers the NYC metro, Fairfield County, and surrounding areas until 9 PM, with SPC carrying a slight risk for severe weather and isolated-to-scattered damaging wind gusts. Grid-scale CAPE sits at 2740 J/kg, but convective-allowing model guidance in the AFD runs notably juicier, 3000-4500 J/kg, and 0-6km shear is a well-organized 26 kt from the WSW — enough to support sustained, potentially severe cells rather than quick pulse storms. On radar, cells are lined up 10-20 miles WNW through NNW of the cove, closing at 15-17 kt.

Normally the Sound gives Riverside and the cove a break: when the air-water temperature gap clears about 10°F with a favorable storm approach, a stable marine layer can choke low-level convective fuel before it reaches shore. Tonight that gate isn't cleared — the gap is 9.0°F, just under the threshold, so the mechanism is not active. Even the modest marine layer sitting there now keeps thinning as the evening air cools: the gap drops below the workable 5°F mark by about 7:13 PM and is down to roughly 1°F by 8 PM. The sea breeze isn't running strongly enough at the moment to offer any opposition either, so neither of the cove's usual local modifiers is in play tonight.

Practically, that means don't expect Riverside and the cove to be spared what Fairfield County and points inland see tonight. The nearest closing cells arrive well before either local mechanism could matter even if it were engaged, so treat the regional severe watch at face value here — wind, rain, and possible damaging gusts should hit the cove much as they hit everywhere else nearby.

The lead cell is centered about 10 miles WNW of the cove, closing at 17 kt, radar-tracked with high confidence: expected arrival 6:25 PM, window 6:15-6:35 PM. A second wave follows close behind, 13 miles NW, arriving around 6:32-6:53 PM, and a broken tail extends the threat out toward 15-20 miles with cells still closing. Given the AFD frames this as a line tracking through 10 PM, treat tonight as a multi-wave event rather than a single quick pass — don't stand down after the first cell clears.

What would change the call: if the line weakens, bows south, or loses reflectivity before crossing the Sound, the risk eases toward moderate. If an upstream APRS station west of the cove shows a gust spike before 6:25 PM, that confirms the line is on schedule or running early — worth a live check as the window opens.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 10 mi WNW closing at 17 kt, first of a broken line tracking through the evening; the marine layer isn't engaged tonight (gap just under threshold), so expect it close to full strength.

wind.tactics_blurb: Steady S-SSW sea breeze (8-9 kt) reinforced by a light onshore gradient holds through the early window, but a broken line of strong-to-severe storms tracking in from the WNW is expected to interrupt it hard between roughly 6:15 and 8 PM — don't commit to a side, be ready to reef or come off the water if the cell closes as forecast.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
DeltaT (west-LIS inland air vs Sound water) is 9°F, clearing the 5°F sea-breeze gate, and the western Long Island Sound station cluster — RYC plus the CT-coast APRS ring — shows a strong, coherent southerly consensus: 90% of west-zone stations southerly with 0.8 direction agreement. The full-network fraction looks weaker (57%) only because it's diluted by an unrelated Long Island north-shore cell that hasn't flipped; for cove purposes the western LIS sea breeze is clearly running. The background gradient is also light and onshore (NWS: S around 6 mph), reinforcing rather than opposing the thermal — this is a sea breeze reinforced by the background wind.

HRRR's model direction is running behind the mature sea breeze: its first forecast hour has SSE 161° while stations are already at S 189°, a 28° divergence. A deltaT-scaled maturation correction of +15° brings the model call to S 176° — trust the observed/corrected direction over raw HRRR for the early window. RYC itself reads S 173° at 8.8 kt (10-min avg 6.6 kt, gusting 11) right now.

The overriding story for this window, though, is the thunderstorm line closing on the cove during these same hours (see the storm assessment) — first cells arriving 6:15-6:55 PM. Expect the clean S/SSW sea-breeze flow to be broken up by gusty, potentially damaging convective outflow as the line crosses, most likely in the 6-8 PM stretch. HRRR's own hour-by-hour forecast shows this directly: a lull, then a shift to W around 13 kt by 8 PM (a post-frontal push) before falling light and variable out of the NW/SW after 9 PM as the line clears east.

Where pressure sits: while the S/SSW sea breeze holds (roughly 5-6 PM), expect fairly uniform, clean flow up the cove axis with no strong side bias. Once the line moves through, don't bank on a repeatable pattern — plan on gusty, directionally unstable conditions through the disruption, then a light, near-calm postfrontal air mass after about 9 PM.

Bottom line: this isn't a night to trust the "reinforced sea breeze holds late" pattern a clean A+ evening would normally promise — the storm line supersedes it. Good breeze early, real risk mid-window, fading air late.

data_caveats: 5:00 PM row uses live RYC/ensemble observations, not HRRR model output — the 21Z HRRR cycle's first forecast hour begins at 6 PM local.
HRRR f07-f12 unavailable (fetch/parse warnings); doesn't affect this window since f01-f05 fully cover 6-10 PM.
AFD convective-allowing model guidance cites CAPE 3000-4500 J/kg, notably higher than the HRRR grid-point value used (2740 J/kg) — model spread on a high-instability evening, not a data error.
